result.summary: Apollo finishes his reconciliation with Hermes by giving him the winged bee-maidens of Parnassus, who give oracles. Zeus confirms Hermes' powers over animals and makes him messenger to Hades, and the hymn closes with a farewell.

scenes.title: Apollo gives the bee-maidens
scenes.summary: Apollo describes three winged virgins near Parnassus who teach divination and speak truth when fed honey. He gives them to Hermes and entrusts him with herds.

scenes.title: Zeus confirms Hermes' honours
scenes.summary: Zeus grants Hermes rule over animals and the office of messenger to Hades. The poet notes Hermes' ambiguous nature and bids farewell.

notable_quotes.reason: Sums up Hermes' trickster nature: he cheats mortals by night.

analysis.text: The ending settles Hermes' place among the gods, giving him real offices and ending his conflict with Apollo.
The bee-maidens reflect Greek ideas of honey-linked prophecy and the oracular tradition around Parnassus and Delphi.

fun_facts.text: The bee-maidens are called Thriae in later sources, and later writers linked them with a form of divination by pebbles.

language_notes.text: "Luck-bringing genius of the gods" addresses Hermes as the divine giver of good fortune; "genius" here means a spirit or power, not intellect.
These winged maidens are the Thriae, prophetic bee-nymphs of Parnassus. The odd detail of white meal sprinkled on their heads is linked to their divination.
"Inspired" means filled with divine prophetic power; the honey acts like an intoxicant that loosens truthful speech.
"Birds of omen" are birds whose flight or cries were read as signs of the gods' will.
"Cozens" means cheats or deceives, recalling Hermes' role as trickster and patron of thieves.

context_notes.text: Apollo, god of prophecy, says he first learned divination as a youth herding cattle; his father Zeus took no notice of it.
Hades is god of the underworld. Hermes guides souls there as psychopomp, the only god who travels freely between the living and the dead.
"Son of Cronos" is Zeus, whose father was the Titan Cronos.

literary_notes.text: Truth when fed on honey and falsehood when deprived sets two opposite states side by side, making the bee-maidens' unreliability vivid.
The long list of beasts and domains conveys the breadth of Hermes' authority and gives the passage a formal, epic dignity.
The poet's blunt remark that Hermes helps little but deceives men by night sums up his ambiguous, trickster nature.
The farewell and promise of another song is the conventional way a Homeric Hymn ends, linking the hymn to the poet's wider performance.
